questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I mainly chose destination based on a desire to live in a "smaller" European city (ie "non-capital-sized"). This excludes several popular destinations such as Paris, Rome, Barcelona etc.

Secondly, I also chose destination based on academic opportunities - and the Toulouse School of Economics ranks really well it its field (Economics of course).

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The experience was great. Toulouse is a perfectly sized city to be in as a student, somewhere in between Århus and København. I of course made sure to buy a bike as early as possible, making almost everything accessible within 15 minutes. Also, the city is pretty flat, which is good in this regard.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
Horrible before arrival, as the faculty was on holidays almost all of august.
But after arriving, it was definitely easier, and the mobility team are pretty helpful.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was a presentation meeting which went through most of the formalities. I recommend writing down all the relevent contact info given at this meeting, and making sure you can find the Erasmus offices in the Arsenal building (right above the cafeteria).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It was definitely not easy - mostly because we were a group of 5 trying to find accomodation together.
But it worked out fine.

I recommend talking to the Erasmus Student Network as soon as possible, as I know they have just started an offer specifically for Erasmus students to get housing. Also utilize the many WhatsApp groups they have to find housemates or such.

There are also facebook groups for Expats in Toulouse. Post a question in there on where to find housing, and the members will help you.

I would recommend starting this process ahead of arrival, as a lot of rooms become available when the previous semester ends. This is the time where you want to get in touch with people looking for tenants.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Off campus is great. Everyone I made friends with lived off campus, so I dont really have anything to say about that.
But as mentioned, the city is not that big. And if you have a bike, you will be pretty mobile.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Honestly nothing about it was really "hard", but the French.... They LOVE paperwork, and you are required to show up for several things before being properly registered. Furthermore, I waited a long time to actually receive my student card - which I got even after I had my first midterm exam.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
There was an office for Erasmus students (right above the cafeteria inside the Arsenal building, room 100-something) where you could show up and ask questions. But the receptionist didn't know that much, and the more knowing staff (such as Lucie Jando) are usually a bit busy. But they are always able to help.

If you are at Toulouse School of Economics specifically, Genevieve Duomeng is also extremely kind and helpful. She is in the TSE building, through the door to the left of the reception and down a long hallway.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I got almost none of the classes I applied for from home, but the staff at TSE was very accomodating, and let me choose some pretty cool Master 2 courses not usually available for Erasmus students. Although you have to convince them that you are ready for the more advanced stuff.
Talk to Genevieve (TSE) as soon as possible to open these options - maybe even before arrival.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Get it done as soon as you arrive, otherwise you will spent too much time worrying about it. Talk to Lucie Jando about anything registration related, and Genevieve Duomeng with anything specific to Economics courses.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I think the levels are pretty appropriate at the masters courses, with the exception of the Macro course. This is roughly equivalent to Macro II at UCPH, and thus not that challenging if you already nailed that one. BUT with that said, keep up with classes - or the midterm exam of that course will overwhelm you (as it seems designed to do so) and it affects your final score.
Generally the 2 ECTS courses seemed easier, but dont underestimate them. Study during the semester, as your exams will be really close (I had 4 exams in 1 week)

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Generally they require you to study more yourself, and participate actively in classes. Some of my M2 courses, we even got partially graded on whether we asked questions and participated in class discussions during the year.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Macroeconomics (M1)
Market Power and Regulations (M1)
Understanding Real World Organizations (M1)
Causal Inference with observational data (M2)
Fundamentals and Policies for a Greener Economy (M2)
Sustainable Development (M2)
Valuing the Environment (M2)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
- As mentioned, the macro course is basically a recap of Macro II at UCPH.
- Market Power was a great brief introduction course to the issues of regulation of international monopolies and such, and a very relevant topic today. The professor is really nice as well.
- Understanding Real World Organizations is very is in the Economics sense, but a very interesting course about how different organizations work - from firms, to platforms (Uber etc.) and and terrorist organizations. Really great British professor (who also teaches second half of Causal Inference)
- Causal is a great course if you like applied Econometrics. It can be very technical, so keep calm and stick to the stuff. Second half was taught by my favorite professor.
- Fundamentals was basically a micro course which includes fundamentals for green economies. This includes green taxes, subsidies, and such. Professor was OK.
 - Sustainable was the macro equivalent of the above, which went through several macro models with sustainability included. The teaching is very mathmatical, but the exam is not so much. So dont spent time writing all the math, just listen to the intutition when the professor takes a break from the math. The professor was this insanely knowledgeable old guy, and I really enjoyed his classes - when I learned to not focus on the math. Score was split between a written exam (which was mostly intutition heavy) and a presentation of a topic you can freely choose yourself. It does not need to include any of the specific course syllabus - as long as it has something to do with the course in general. I really liked that
- Valuing is a practical course about how to conduct research designs to value non-market goods such as a good environment etc. The course is taught by a Swedish professor with a lot of research background, and part of the course was to conduct a Stated Preference study with actual respondents. Really cool experience. (BUT remember to participate in class and keep deadlines - he is very strict with that)

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Not really anything. I bought a bike on facebook marketplace for 50 Euros, which I had to fix a little during the mobility. Around 20 euros in maintenance.
My housemates used the bike rental service, I dont remember the name at the moment. The one with blue front tires on their bikes, also present here in Copenhagen

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Groceries were more expensive than expected
But eating out was cheaper.
And the wine..... You can get reeeeally good wine for amazing prices. I recommend Midi Minuit, Buvette, Le Volcan and La Bonne Combine for this. There are several other places, but those I used the most.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Several, but I did not participate. Not much of a sports guy.

But Toulouse has several great restaurants and bars, which I used frequently. And go watch soccer or rugby games at the stadium, it has a great atmosphere (even for a non-sports-person such as me)

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
- Buvette (nice beers and wine bottles. Wines by glass was a bit boring)
- Midi Minuit (great family style servings, and excellent wine selection)
- Ginette (close to the house I lived in. Amazing local bar with all types present. Not very student like, more local)
- Le Petit Voisin (cheap beers and drinks, very popular with younger people. Best watering hole close to center)
- Le Concorde (Really great old bar, very nice staff and great drinks. Drink a negroni for me!)
- Le Volcan (this place is so special. Really small room with an old guy selling wine at amazing prices. Smoking inside!)
- Cafe Populaire (Cheapest beers in the city, great place if you are a large group looking to get drunk. Also, just walking distance from some of the great clubs (limelight etc.)
- La Fiancée (one of the only places in the city with proper filter coffee (non-espresso), pour-over and aeropress. Best staff in town as well. Miss those guys)
- Nasdrovia (Great high end cocktails, but you will pay extra for it!)
- The boat with the nightclub in it. (dont remember the name of the place, but it is located in the small canal some 100's of meters west of Manufacture de Tabacs. Only place I found where they play non-pop electronic music)
- Titanium (If you are looking to get piercings!)
- Restaurant sans nom (best place I ate - but there are really many good places I never tried)
- The Hopscotch (local brewed beers, scottish style. The bartender is really cool, even though he looks a bit like Ed Kemper)
- Syrabite Vintage (for vintage shoppoing)
- 43 Original Barber shop (for haircuts)
- Mak Food or Boui Boui (for the best Kebabs)

Cant remember much else. Ask the staff for recommendations every time you go to a place you like!
Oh yeah eat a Cassoulet! Best local dish they offer in town (and STAY AWAY FROM THE VEAL LIVER DISH!)
Oh ye

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Keep and eye on cheap tickets for Flixbus. And french train tickets are sometimes on 1€ offers! The Erasmus Network WhatsApp channels are great for keeping up with this.
Also, get the app getaround if you want to rent a car. Prices are really great, and the app works well. But register beforehand, as they have to approve your drivers licence manually before you can drive!

Go to Biarritz, Bordeaux Lyon and Carcassonne, and maybe even Barcelona. 

My personal favorite trip was renting a car, and driving to the Pyrenees for hiking. The area is amazing.
Check the internet for hiking routes beforehand, so you know how tough they are, and how long they will take.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Rather easy. France is still Europe. Language is really hard though, and they are not the best at English.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
This is tough, as you will mostly meet exchange students.
If you enroll in M2 courses like me, you will be closer to the local students - especially if the course has group work. Use this! Invite them for beers, and have talks with them.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
The French are generally not great at English, but most young people speak it. 
The hardest adjustment is how late they eat dinner, and that many stores close for a couple of hours each day. But if you ever vacationed anywhere in southern Europe, you already know this.

Other than that, mostly the obsession with paperwork amazed me. And the weird kebabs they make (nan-bread with melted cheese? Tortillas with chicken and french fries? Thats not a taco!)
With that said, eat the local kebab. Those guys always speak english as well.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The food and wine, definitely. Eat lots of local food, and buy wines by the bottle when you eat out!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Be patient with the university staff. They are slow and like their paperworks, but was generally really understanding.
- Keep up with classes during the semester, otherwise you will die in the exam period
- Have tons of fun. Check my recommendations list above.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: See above

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
Having all the enviromental courses was great and very academically rewarding
Going out with other Erasmus students was very socially rewarding.

And also, remember to invite friends/girlfriends from home to visit you! Its really fun to show them around a city like a "local".

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The... God... Damn... Paperwork!

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Not really - just have fun, drink lots of local wine, and get a bike!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
